question: Best fractional CRO for a biotech company?
body:
## Direct Answer
The best fractional CRO for a biotech company is one who pairs a proven life-sciences commercialization record with fluency in the FDA-gated revenue timeline — someone who can build a launch-ready commercial engine before approval, not just close deals after it. Prioritize operators who have carried a therapeutic or diagnostic product from pre-revenue through first commercial launch, understand payer and reimbursement dynamics, and can scale a team on a part-time cadence that matches your clinical milestones. There is no single "best" name; the best fit is milestone-matched, therapeutic-area-aware, and structurally aligned to your burn rate.

Biotech is not SaaS with a lab coat. Revenue is throttled by regulatory approval, buying is governed by reimbursement and formulary access, and the sales motion may run through KOLs, GPOs, health systems, or channel distributors rather than a self-serve funnel. A fractional Chief Revenue Officer lets a Series A-to-C biotech buy senior commercial judgment — go-to-market design, pricing, market access, and early team build — without committing to a full C-suite salary and equity load years before product revenue exists. This essay lays out how to define the role, where to source candidates, how to vet for biotech-specific competence, and how to structure the engagement so it survives the long pre-revenue runway.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a pre-revenue biotech?
For most biotechs, the fractional CRO arrives long before there is meaningful revenue to run. That inverts the usual expectation. In a growth-stage software company, a CRO inherits a pipeline and is measured on bookings this quarter. In biotech, the fractional CRO is often hired at Phase 2 or Phase 3 to architect the commercial organization that will exist at launch — building the market-access strategy, the pricing and gross-to-net model, the field-force sizing, and the KOL engagement plan that must be ready the day the FDA decision letter arrives. The deliverable is readiness, not immediate bookings.

That means the role blends commercial strategy with operational scaffolding. A strong fractional CRO for biotech will define the target product profile's commercial implications, map the payer and provider ecosystem for the indication, model the addressable population against realistic reimbursement scenarios, and stand up the earliest revenue operations infrastructure — CRM, territory design, incentive compensation frameworks, and the data spine that will feed forecasting. They also serve as the commercial voice in the room during clinical and regulatory strategy discussions, ensuring the trial endpoints and label language you fight for are the ones payers and prescribers will actually pay for. For companies further along — a diagnostics or medtech firm already selling — the fractional CRO looks more conventional: fixing a stalled pipeline, rebuilding the commercial team, or driving a repeatable revenue motion. The common thread is senior commercial ownership scaled to a part-time, milestone-driven cadence. For the underlying economics of buying senior leadership by the fraction, see [the fractional executive model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10842).

## What separates a great biotech fractional CRO from a generic one?
The single biggest failure mode is hiring a brilliant generalist revenue leader who has never operated inside a regulated, reimbursement-gated market. Biotech commercialization has structural features that do not exist in most B2B selling, and a CRO who does not natively understand them will burn six months learning what a seasoned life-sciences operator already knows. The four features that matter most are market access, the KOL-driven adoption curve, the regulatory-commercial interface, and the specifics of the buying ecosystem for your modality.

Market access is the discipline of securing payer coverage, favorable formulary placement, and a reimbursement pathway — and in many indications it determines revenue far more than the field sales team does. A great biotech fractional CRO has personally navigated payer negotiations, value-dossier construction, and the gross-to-net erosion that turns a headline price into realized net revenue. The KOL and advisory-board dynamic is equally distinctive: early adoption in specialty therapeutics runs through a small number of key opinion leaders whose endorsement shapes prescribing behavior, so the CRO must know how to build medical-affairs-adjacent relationships without crossing compliance lines. The regulatory-commercial interface means the CRO understands what promotional claims a label permits, how off-label rules constrain the sales conversation, and how the timing of an FDA advisory committee or PDUFA date reshapes the entire commercial calendar. Finally, the buying ecosystem differs sharply by modality — a rare-disease therapeutic sells to a handful of academic centers, a diagnostic sells to health-system labs and pathologists, a medical device sells through GPO contracts and value-analysis committees. Ask any candidate to whiteboard the exact buying journey for your product; the generalist will describe a generic funnel, and the specialist will name the actual stakeholders and the sequence in which they say yes. This is why sourcing from the right pool matters more than raw revenue résumé strength — a point we return to in [vetting revenue leaders for domain fit](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10915).

## Where should a biotech source a fractional CRO?
There are five practical channels, and the right one depends on your stage, cash position, and how much hand-holding your board wants. The channels differ in cost, speed, and the depth of vetting they provide, so it helps to weigh them explicitly rather than defaulting to whichever introduction lands first.

Life-sciences-focused executive search and interim firms — Bespoke Partners, Danforth Advisors, and similar life-sciences-specialized firms — offer the deepest vetting and the best odds of a genuine therapeutic-area match, at the highest cost and slowest pace. Fractional-executive networks and marketplaces such as Chief Outsiders or Bolster surface part-time commercial leaders quickly and at lower cost, but you must screen hard for real biotech depth versus generic B2B experience. Venture and board networks are often the highest-signal channel: your lead investor has likely watched a dozen portfolio launches and can name the operator who saved one of them — warm, pre-vetted, and frequently the fastest path to a strong hire. Interim-executive and turnaround firms fit when you need a specific gap filled on a defined clock, such as bridging between a departed CRO and a permanent hire. Finally, direct outreach to recently-exited operators — commercial leaders whose companies were just acquired and who are between full-time roles — can land exceptional talent, though it requires you to run your own diligence. Whatever the channel, insist on references from people who watched the candidate operate through an actual launch or commercial inflection, not just from people who liked working with them.

## How do you structure and price the engagement?
Because a biotech fractional CRO is often hired years before revenue, the engagement structure has to survive a long pre-revenue runway without either bankrupting the company or under-motivating the operator. The two levers are time commitment and compensation mix, and both should be tied to clinical and commercial milestones rather than to a flat monthly retainer that quietly drains a cash-constrained balance sheet.

On time, be honest about intensity. A pre-launch strategy build might genuinely need only one to two days per week, ramping toward launch as the field organization stands up. Trying to run a full commercial launch on a one-day-a-week fractional arrangement is a common and costly mistake — as the launch window approaches, the role either converts to full-time or the company hires a permanent CRO underneath the fractional strategist. Structure the contract with an explicit ramp and a defined conversion trigger so nobody is surprised. On compensation, the typical mix is a cash day-rate or monthly retainer plus equity, weighted toward equity precisely because pre-revenue biotech is cash-poor and upside-rich; the equity aligns the operator with the launch outcome they are being hired to secure. Avoid fabricated market "standard" rates — the right number depends on therapeutic area, the operator's track record, and your stage, so benchmark against two or three real comparable engagements rather than a blog-post figure. Tie a meaningful slice of the economics to milestone deliverables: market-access plan approved, launch team hired, first payer contract signed. For a deeper treatment of aligning part-time leadership incentives to outcomes, see [structuring fractional engagements](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10967).

The other structural question is governance. A fractional CRO who reports cleanly to the CEO, sits in on board commercial reviews, and has a defined decision-rights boundary will outperform one who is treated as an outside consultant whose deck gets politely filed. Give the role real authority over the commercial plan, the hiring of the launch team, and the go-to-market budget within agreed limits. The whole point of buying senior judgment by the fraction is to let that judgment actually steer decisions.

## How do you measure whether the fractional CRO is working?
The measurement trap in biotech is obvious: you cannot judge a pre-revenue commercial leader on revenue. So you need leading indicators that predict launch success, and you need to agree on them before the engagement starts. The right scorecard mixes deliverable milestones, ecosystem-readiness signals, and team-build progress, reviewed on the same cadence as your board meetings.

Deliverable milestones are the backbone: is the market-access strategy complete and board-approved, is the pricing and gross-to-net model built and stress-tested, is the launch playbook documented, are the payer value dossiers drafted. Ecosystem-readiness signals tell you whether the market is being prepared — KOL advisory boards convened, early payer conversations initiated, health-system or channel partners identified and warmed. Team-build progress measures whether the commercial organization that must exist at launch is actually coming together — key hires identified and closed, CRM and revenue-operations infrastructure stood up, incentive-comp framework designed. Once the product is approved and selling, the scorecard shifts fast toward conventional revenue metrics: net revenue against forecast, coverage and reimbursement wins, prescriber or account adoption, and sales-cycle velocity. The discipline that matters is agreeing in advance which metrics govern which phase, so a strong pre-launch operator is not unfairly judged on bookings that the regulatory calendar has not yet unlocked. For a broader framework on the metrics that actually predict commercial launch outcomes, see [revenue leading indicators](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q11021).

## When should a biotech convert from fractional to full-time?
The fractional arrangement is a bridge, and the most common strategic error is riding it too long past the point where a full-time commercial leader is warranted. The conversion signal is rarely a single event; it is the convergence of approaching launch, a commercial team large enough to need daily leadership, and a revenue trajectory that justifies — and can fund — a full C-suite salary.

Practically, the trigger tends to arrive around the time an FDA decision looks probable and the field organization moves from planning to hiring. At that point the role's intensity outruns a part-time cadence, and the company faces a choice: convert the sitting fractional CRO to full-time if they want the seat and fit the long-term culture, or use the fractional operator to help recruit and onboard the permanent CRO they will hand off to. Both paths are legitimate. What you should avoid is drifting — keeping a one-day-a-week arrangement in place while a live commercial launch quietly demands five. Build the conversion decision into the engagement from day one, with an honest conversation about whether the operator wants the full-time role and whether you want them in it. The best fractional CROs are often explicit that they are bridge operators who prefer to hand off at scale, and knowing that upfront lets you plan the succession rather than scramble through it.

## Related questions
### Do biotechs even need a CRO before launch?
Yes for anything beyond a pure research play. A pre-revenue commercial leader builds the market-access, pricing, and launch-readiness infrastructure that takes 18–24 months to stand up — starting at approval is starting too late.

### Fractional CRO vs fractional CCO — what's the difference in biotech?
Titles blur, but a Chief Commercial Officer typically owns the full commercial function including marketing and medical-affairs coordination, while a CRO centers on revenue, sales, and market access. In small biotechs one fractional operator often covers both.

### How is a biotech CRO different from a pharma CRO?
Scale and stage. A large-pharma commercial leader inherits an established access machine and brand portfolio; a biotech fractional CRO builds the first commercial engine from scratch under capital constraints and a single-product bet.

### Can one fractional CRO serve multiple biotechs at once?
Commonly yes, and it can be a strength — cross-portfolio pattern recognition on payer strategy is valuable. Guard against conflicts within the same therapeutic area and confirm they have real bandwidth as your launch approaches.

### What therapeutic-area fit actually matters?
Payer and buying dynamics cluster by area — rare disease, oncology, and specialty biologics each have distinct access and channel patterns. A candidate with adjacent-area launch experience usually transfers well; a candidate with none in regulated markets rarely does.

## FAQ
**How much does a fractional CRO for a biotech cost?**
It varies widely by therapeutic area, the operator's track record, and your stage, and it is usually a cash day-rate or monthly retainer plus equity weighted toward the launch outcome. Benchmark against two or three real comparable engagements rather than a published "standard" figure, which rarely reflects your specific situation.

**How many days a week should a biotech fractional CRO work?**
Often one to two days during pre-launch strategy build, ramping toward full-time intensity as the launch window and field-team hiring approach. Structure an explicit ramp and a conversion trigger into the contract so the arrangement scales with the workload.

**What's the biggest risk in hiring a fractional CRO for biotech?**
Hiring a strong generalist revenue leader with no experience in regulated, reimbursement-gated markets. They lose months learning market access, KOL dynamics, and the regulatory-commercial interface that a seasoned life-sciences operator already knows cold.

**Should the fractional CRO have launched a product in my exact indication?**
Ideally in your indication, acceptably in an adjacent therapeutic area with similar payer and channel dynamics. What is non-negotiable is at least one hands-on commercialization or launch in a regulated life-sciences market.

**How do I vet a fractional CRO's biotech experience?**
Ask them to whiteboard the exact buying journey and payer pathway for your product — a specialist names the real stakeholders and sequence, a generalist describes a generic funnel. Then take references from people who watched them operate through an actual launch or commercial inflection.

**When do I convert to a full-time CRO?**
When approaching approval, a growing commercial team, and a fundable revenue trajectory converge — typically as an FDA decision looks probable and field hiring begins. Build the conversion decision into the engagement from the start rather than drifting on a part-time cadence into a live launch.

**Can a fractional CRO help us raise our next round?**
Frequently yes. A credible commercial leader and a rigorous market-access and revenue-forecast model materially strengthen the commercial narrative investors scrutinize, and their presence signals launch seriousness to a board and to prospective Series B or C investors.

**What should be in the fractional CRO's first-90-days plan?**
A commercial assessment of the target product profile, a mapped payer and provider ecosystem for the indication, a first-pass pricing and gross-to-net model, an early market-access strategy, and a prioritized list of the launch-team hires and revenue-operations infrastructure to stand up next.
